Aiproductmanagement Aiagents Product Strategy Techcareers Product Management If I Were Learning AI Product Management Today, I’d Start Here Arushi Rana 4 min read · Oct 24, 2026 -- Listen Share Eight essential skills to move from understanding AI to building products with it. AI product management is evolving faster than traditional product development frameworks can keep up. Understanding user needs, defining roadmaps, and prioritizing features still matter. But building AI-powered products requires an additional layer of expertise: knowing how the technology works, choosing the right architecture, evaluating model behavior, and translating technical capabilities into measurable business outcomes. If I were building my AI Product Management skill set from scratch today, I would focus on these eight areas. Press enter or click to view image in full size 1. AI Foundations: ML vs. LLMs Not every problem requires an LLM. Some are better solved using traditional machine learning, rules-based systems, or simpler automation. An AI product manager should understand the trade-offs between these approaches, including accuracy, latency, cost, explainability, and maintenance. Focus on: Understanding the problem first, then selecting the appropriate technology. 2. Understanding How LLMs Work Prompting is only one part of working with large language models. Learn the fundamentals of tokens, context windows, attention, inference, hallucinations, and model limitations. Explore how prompt design and context engineering influence the quality of outputs. Focus on: Understanding why a model behaves a certain way, not just how to write a better prompt. 3. Tools, Integrations and MCP AI systems become more useful when they can interact with external tools, retrieve information, and execute actions. Learn how tool calling works, how APIs connect systems, and how the Model Context Protocol (MCP) can help models interact with compatible tools and resources. Focus on: Understanding the integration, permissions, security, and reliability considerations behind AI-powered workflows. 4. AI Agents and Skills Agents can combine language models with tools, instructions, memory, and multi-step execution to accomplish tasks. Explore the difference between a simple chatbot, a tool-using assistant, and an agentic workflow. Understand when autonomy adds value and when a predictable, predefined workflow is the better choice. Focus on: Designing agents around clear objectives, bounded permissions, and reliable outcomes. 5. Orchestration and Routing As AI systems become more sophisticated, product teams must decide how tasks are distributed across models, tools, workflows, or multiple agents. Learn about model routing, task decomposition, workflow orchestration, failure recovery, and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Focus on: Choosing the simplest architecture that meets the product’s requirements without introducing unnecessary complexity. 6. RAG and Context Engineering A model’s answer is only as useful as the information available to it. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) helps systems retrieve relevant external information to support responses. Context engineering takes a broader view of how instructions, retrieved data, conversation history, and other relevant information are assembled for a model. Understand embeddings, chunking, retrieval quality, citations, freshness, and the trade-offs between RAG and fine-tuning. Focus on: Giving the model the right information at the right time. 7. Evals, Grounding and Observability AI quality cannot be established through a successful demo alone. Product managers need ways to evaluate outputs systematically, identify failure patterns, and monitor behavior after launch. Learn how to create evaluation datasets, define scoring criteria, assess groundedness, use human review, and monitor latency, cost, quality, and safety. Focus on: Establishing measurable quality thresholds before launch and monitoring them in production. 8. Technical Interviews and Product Communication Technical knowledge becomes valuable when you can apply it to real product decisions and explain your reasoning clearly. Practice AI product sense, system design, model selection, architecture trade-offs, evaluation strategy, and prioritization under constraints. Be prepared to explain not only what you would build, but why you would build it that way, how you would measure success, and what you would do if the system failed. Focus on: Connecting technical depth with user value, business impact, and sound product judgment. Turn knowledge into proof Reading guides is a useful starting point. Applying what you learn is what makes the difference. Choose one meaningful product problem and build a portfolio project around it. Document the problem statement, user research, architecture choices, prototype, evaluation methodology, cost considerations, rollout strategy, and measurable outcomes. Your portfolio should demonstrate how you think, what you can build, and how you make decisions when the technology has limitations. You do not need to master every AI concept before you begin.
